title: Epigenetics: Switching Genes On and Off
hook: Two cells can carry identical DNA yet behave completely differently — because chemical tags decide which genes are switched on, without touching the code itself.
key_points: Epigenetics is about controlling gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
Chemical tags on DNA and its packaging proteins turn genes on or off.
It explains how one genome produces many specialized cell types.
Some epigenetic marks respond to environment and can sometimes be inherited.
content_html: Every cell in your body shares the same DNA, so how does a skin cell end up so different from a neuron? The answer is epigenetics: a layer of control that decides which genes get used in each cell, without altering the genetic code itself. It's the difference between owning a cookbook and choosing which recipes to actually cook.
extra_html: Epigenetic control works through chemical tags placed on the DNA or on the proteins that DNA wraps around. These tags can switch genes on or off or dial their activity up and down, which is how a single genome gives rise to hundreds of specialized cell types. As the NIH's genetics glossary describes, what makes epigenetics especially intriguing is that some of these marks respond to the environment — diet, stress, exposures — and a few can even be passed to the next generation. Throughout, the DNA sequence stays untouched; only the pattern of which genes are read changes.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

related.title: From DNA to Protein: The Central Dogma
related.hook: Your DNA is a recipe book locked in the nucleus — so the cell copies a single recipe to RNA, carries it out, and reads it to build a protein.

related.title: Mutations: When DNA Changes
related.hook: Every time a cell copies its DNA, tiny typos can slip in — most do nothing at all, a few cause disease, and rare ones fuel evolution.

related.title: CRISPR: Molecular Scissors for DNA
related.hook: Borrowed from a bacterial immune system, CRISPR lets scientists find a precise spot in the genome and cut it — turning gene editing into something almost routine.

flashcards.prompt: What does epigenetics control, and what does it leave unchanged?
flashcards.back_html: It controls which genes are turned on or off (gene expression) without changing the underlying DNA sequence itself.

flashcards.prompt: How does a skin cell and a nerve cell differ if they share the same DNA?

choices.text: Different genes are switched on in each, an epigenetic effect
They actually have completely different DNA sequences
Skin cells have no DNA at all

flashcards.explanation_html: They carry the same genome but express different genes. Epigenetic marks determine which genes are active, giving each cell type its identity.

flashcards.prompt: Which statement about epigenetic marks is true?

choices.text: Some respond to the environment and can occasionally be inherited
They permanently rewrite the DNA sequence
They are fixed at birth and never change

flashcards.explanation_html: Epigenetic marks can shift in response to environment and lifestyle, and some can even be passed to offspring — yet the DNA sequence stays the same.
